analysis.title: US Energy: Megawatts, Molecules & Minerals: They Expect One of Us in the Wreckage, Brother — Buying Duration Sensitive Stocks
key_insights: The 3Q 2026 selloff in the 10-year Treasury was more than 80bps, one of the worst quarters for bonds in 30+ years, while CPI stayed generally subdued and growth kept running.

The author's closest historical analog is 1997. The Fed made 175bp of cuts between September 2024 and December 2025 without a recession or credit event, and the author compares that with the 1995-96 'insurance cuts'.
In 1997 a ~50bp 10-year selloff in 1Q97 preceded a March 1997 'preemptive' hike, the only hike of that cycle. Yields peaked about 3 weeks after the hike.
After the March 1997 hike the 10-year rallied ~40bp in the following quarter and ~250bp more after that. The S&P rose ~17% in 2Q97. Headline CPI fell back to ~2.2% by May 1997 from a ~3.3% peak.

Revised data showed 1990s productivity growth was higher than first estimated, rising from 1.6% to 2.5%, which vindicated Greenspan's view. The author draws a parallel to AI-driven productivity in 2026 and sees a bond rally as possible.
The author ranks plays on a bond rally by torque, most to least: recent energy IPOs, solar/renewables, gold, utilities.

Recent power-linked energy IPOs under JPM coverage are down ~30% from IPO price on average. Many, especially SMRs, are long-duration stories hurt by higher discount rates. Other pressures include looming lockups, politics and overcapacity concerns.

The recent energy IPOs covered average ~20% short interest as a % of float, which gives squeeze torque in a rally. INIO is the largest at $15bn market cap. The Russell has been up in 9 of the past 10 fourth quarters, averaging +5.5%.

Solar (TAN) underperformed the S&P by the widest margin since 2015 in 3Q, even as Democrat odds of taking the Senate rose from ~40% to 65%. Idiosyncratic drags include the inverter executive order, Section 232 ambiguity and potential demand destruction.

Residential solar has the most rate torque. Consumer investment in residential solar, batteries and zero-emission vehicles led clean energy spending in 2Q26, up 45% sequentially and 21% y/y per Rhodium. The utility-scale solar/storage basket is down 50% from its June peak.
FT data cited: new solar and wind capacity will rise by 30% and 50% respectively in 2026 despite OBBB tax credit cuts.

The author has been a gold skeptic most of the year but now sees asymmetric upside. If inflation unanchors, the debasement trade resumes. If it does not, real rates fall. Gold is also a call option on a data center development stall.

The author sees downside support for gold. China is ramping purchases as prices fall, and global gold ETFs added ounces in September even as rates rose. Earlier in the year higher real rates meant ETF outflows.

Gold miners look worth a second look. GDX net flows are about flat on the year after $1bn of outflows over 6 months. JPM's gold miners dashboard cites high single-digit FCF yields and average net cash of ~3% of market cap.

XLU saw its largest 2-week inflow on record, about $2bn, last week. Only 3% of S&P 500 Utility members were above their 200-day moving average, the lowest since 1Q22. The L/S ratio of JPM's JP2UTE basket is in the 4th percentile on an 8-year lookback.

Utilities have a catalyst beyond the macro: 3Q/EEI updates, with JPM research identifying names with potential capex upside versus rate base CAGR needs. CEG (~5% of XLU) lifted sector sentiment after GOOGL news.
This is a Sales & Trading specialist-sales view and not the view of JPM Research, unless explicitly stated.

Beaten down against rising rates. Residential has the most torque, and the utility-scale basket is -50% from its June peak with solid fundamentals.
Several paths to a win: the debasement trade if inflation unanchors, lower real rates if it does not, and a growth call option. China and ETF buying provide support.
Washed-out breadth and positioning, record XLU inflows and a 3Q/EEI capex catalyst.

A cycle-preserving easing with no recession or credit event. The author compares it to the 1995-96 insurance cuts.
Oil-driven headline inflation led Greenspan to hike preemptively in March 1997. It faded to ~2.2% by May 1997.
The pre-hike bond selloff. Yields peaked ~3 weeks after the March 1997 hike.
The rally came in the quarter after the hike, with ~250bp more after that.
A strong equity rally alongside the bond rally, used as the template for a potential 4Q 2026 rally.
Revisions confirmed the productivity story, which is the basis for the AI-productivity parallel.
Cited as the 'white hot' economy that drove the consensus view that real rates head higher.

tension_points.bull_case: A 1997-style preemptive hike followed by a bond rally, with AI productivity keeping inflation contained. The 10-year rallied ~40bp the quarter after the 1997 hike and the S&P rose ~17%.
tension_points.bear_case: The 'guns & butter' parallel suggests an inflation right-tail risk, which would keep rates and the bond selloff going. The 1997 analog is n=1.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Inflation unanchoring. The author notes that in that case the debasement trade resumes and benefits gold.

theme_stances.key_argument: The current selloff after cycle-preserving cuts resembles 1997, when yields peaked within weeks of a preemptive hike and then rallied.
theme_stances.evidence: The closest analog, as far as I can tell, is 1997.

theme_stances.key_argument: Power-linked energy IPOs, solar, gold and utilities would benefit most from a falling-rate backdrop.
theme_stances.evidence: I am hard pressed to think a rally is not afoot if the rate backdrop changes.

theme_stances.key_argument: Gold wins whether inflation unanchors or real rates fall, with China and ETF buying as a floor.
theme_stances.evidence: growth is hot, real rates are heading higher—is consensus now
